video.title: Everyone Ignores this Business, But It Makes $6M/Year

summary: Jay describes building a vending business, then adding coffee service and five-gallon water delivery before focusing on Mountain Glacier, a bottled-water production business. Today he says the business is constrained by production, freight costs, and financing after a difficult robotics installation. David Heacock advises him to understand customer-level profitability and cash flow, simplify freight, and verify what growth would actually earn before expanding. The businesses depend on physical production and delivery, so they offer limited scope for agents to run unattended.

ideas.name: Full-line vending route

ideas.delivery: Jay and his wife started with a route truck and two machines. The operator stocks and services machines, handles routes, and manages cash or electronic payments. Jay says he and his wife were the first two employees and he did sales, route driving, and repairs.
unit_economics_claims: Jay says the vending business reached about $10 million in sales before he exited.
Jay says a vending route needs about $1 million in revenue to support a warehouse and money room and stop the owner from running routes.
Jay warns that financed machines with high interest costs can leave a small operator working nights and weekends without much income.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Jay says he bought his first route truck and received two vending machines.

acquisition.how: The example relied on personal relationships and direct account wins. In-person sales are difficult to automate.

onboarding.how: A system could collect location, product, and access details, but a person would need to assess the site and agree machine placement.

delivery.how: Machines must be physically stocked, repaired, and serviced. Software can monitor sales and stock but cannot do the route work.

billing.how: Payment terminals and accounting software can record transactions, with routine reconciliation and exception checks.

support.how: A human is needed to respond to breakdowns, restocking problems, and customer complaints.

uk_applicability.notes: Vending is an established UK business model. Local site agreements, food safety rules, product sourcing, and payment costs would apply.

risks: Jay says small operators can take on high-interest machine finance and still fail to generate enough income.
The business is physically demanding and is not passive: machines need stocking and servicing.
Cash handling creates waste and theft risk; Jay says operators need technology to reduce it.
Without sufficient route density, travel time and servicing can make the business uneconomic.

ideas.name: Mountain Glacier bottled-water production
ideas.one_liner: Produce and supply five-gallon bottled water, including spring, reverse-osmosis, and blended water, to commercial customers.
ideas.business_model: Manufacturing and supply contracts; Jay describes selling water to distributors and large commercial customers. Exact terms are not stated.
ideas.customer: Water distributors and large commercial customers, including manufacturing plants and regional accounts.
ideas.problem: Customers need a dependable supply of bottled water that meets their product, quality, and delivery requirements.
ideas.offer: Process and bottle water in a regulated plant, test production batches, and supply finished bottles for delivery.

price_points.label: Evansville routes bought from Nestlé Waters

pricing.notes: The $225,000 figure is an acquisition price for routes and a customer list, not a stated selling price for water.

acquisition_channels.details: Jay bought three Evansville routes and a customer list from Nestlé Waters after receiving a broker's fax. The acquired accounts included large industrial customers.

quote.text: In 2006, we bought that customer list and those three routes from Nestle.
quote.speaker: Jay

acquisition_channels.details: Jay used a distributor agreement with Nestlé and backhauled product from Wisconsin Glacier Springs while establishing the Evansville operation.
Jay says his established industry relationships helped him secure water customers and plant opportunities.

ideas.delivery: The plant processes municipal water through filtration, reverse osmosis, UV, and ozonation, or receives spring water by tanker. Water is blended, bottled on a production line, checked, held for batch testing, and shipped. Robotics handle some loading and unloading; employees run, inspect, and maintain production. Freight has historically been handled by Jay's own trucking operation and outside carriers.
unit_economics_claims: Jay says the Evansville route and customer-list acquisition cost $225,000 and generated about $1.1 million in revenue at the time.
Jay says Mountain Glacier currently has about $6 million in sales and produces about two million bottles.
Jay says the plant is producing 40 truckloads per week and can produce 80.
Jay says a full truckload is 920 bottles.
Jay says he needs about $600,000 to address short-term debt and vendor payables; an additional investment could support expansion.
tools: Bottle caps and pallet or bottle handling systems
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated for starting the plant. Jay says he acquired the Evansville routes and customer list for $225,000 and had also invested in a water facility.

acquisition.how: Large accounts and route purchases came through brokers, industry relationships, and negotiations. In-person commercial sales are hard to automate.

onboarding.how: Software could collect specifications, delivery schedules, and compliance documents, with human review of contracts, water recipes, and site requirements.

delivery.how: Robots automate part of loading and unloading, but production still needs operators, testing, maintenance, and physical shipping. The delivery portion requires drivers.

billing.how: Accounting software can automate invoices and payment tracking, with human checks for contract terms, disputes, and cash flow.

support.how: Customer quality issues, production interruptions, and delivery failures require a human to diagnose and resolve.

uk_applicability.notes: The production model can operate in the UK, but it needs UK-specific water, food-safety, workplace, and environmental compliance. Plant investment, route density, and customer contracts would also need local adaptation.

risks: Jay says bottled water is highly regulated and requires quality systems, inspections, and food-safety planning.
A flawed robotics design and a long commissioning period created overtime, missed capacity, and financial strain.
The company relies on a limited number of large customers, so losing a contract could leave dedicated drivers or capacity without work.
Production growth can increase cash needs before cash is collected.
The business has substantial debt and assets pledged as collateral under SBA loans.
Spring water, municipal water, and blended products require different sourcing and quality controls.
Physical production and distribution limit the extent to which agents can run the business without staff.

ideas.one_liner: Operate trucks and trailers to haul bottled water and other freight, either for the owner's business or third parties.

ideas.customer: Manufacturers and freight customers needing truckload transportation.
ideas.problem: Customers need dependable transportation capacity for freight lanes.

ideas.delivery: Drivers use day-cab trucks, sleeper tractors, and trailers to haul freight. Jay says the operation historically served his own water routes and also performed third-party for-hire work. He is selling trucks and trailers and considering a freight partner.

acquisition.how: Winning and negotiating freight lanes relies on relationships, carrier capacity, and contract negotiation.

onboarding.how: Software can collect lane, shipment, and scheduling details, but people must verify equipment, capacity, and customer requirements.

delivery.how: Drivers must physically move freight. Software can route and track loads but cannot replace driving or loading.

billing.how: Freight systems can automate invoices, mileage, fuel surcharges, and proof-of-delivery tracking, with human exception handling.

support.how: Delays, breakdowns, and missed pickups need people to coordinate and resolve them.

uk_applicability.notes: Freight operations exist in the UK, but vehicle rules, driver requirements, insurance, fuel costs, and road networks differ from the US.

risks: Trucks and trailers depreciate, while insurance, fuel, and driver costs can remain high.
Dedicated lanes create risk if a large customer changes its network or cancels with little notice.
Jay describes a slow and painful process to sell trucks and equipment.
Long-term freight contracts can reduce flexibility; David advises negotiating lane rates and keeping carriers accountable.
Physical driving and freight handling prevent unattended operation.
